b.v: 1) German is spelled as it sounds
Unlike English, German almost always sounds the way it is written. Learn the letter rules once and you can read any word aloud, even one you have never seen.
2) The letters that trip people up

v: ch after a, o, u = throaty, like Scottish loch — Buch
ch after e, i = soft, like a hissed h — ich
st / sp at the start = 'sht' / 'shp' — Straße, sprechen

b.v: ei and ie catch everyone. The rule: say the name of the SECOND letter. ei → the second letter is i, so it sounds like 'eye'. ie → the second letter is e, so it sounds like 'ee'.

v: ä — like the e in bed
ß — a double s, never a B
Read all ten out loud twice
Say: Wasser, Straße, Schule, ich, Buch — watch the ch
Greet at any time of day
Know when to say du and when to say Sie
Guten Tag = good day (the safe one, most of the day)
Servus / Grüß Gott = hello in Bavaria and Austria

b.v: German has two words for 'you'. Sie is formal and is used with strangers, older people, shopkeepers, officials. du is for friends, family, children and colleagues who have offered it.

v: Wie geht es Ihnen? = how are you? (formal)
Mir geht es gut, danke = I am well, thank you

b.v: If you are unsure, use Sie. Being too formal is invisible. Being too casual is not.

v: Gute Nacht = good night (only when going to bed)
Es tut mir leid = I am sorry
Danke schön = thank you very much

b.v: About 30 minutes. This is the part of German everyone complains about — and it is not as bad as its reputation.
German nouns are masculine, feminine or neuter, and the word for 'the' changes with it. The gender is not about meaning — a girl, Mädchen, is neuter. You learn the gender with the word, not after it.
Never learn a noun on its own. Learn 'der Tisch', never 'Tisch'. It costs nothing now and saves years later.

v: Ending in -er for a person doing something → der (Lehrer, Fahrer)
Days, months and seasons → der (der Montag, der Mai, der Sommer)

b.v: Every noun in German starts with a capital letter, wherever it sits in the sentence. This is not optional and it is a fast way to spot nouns while reading.

b.v: German says the units before the tens, joined by und. 21 is 'one-and-twenty'.
This is why Germans sometimes pause when writing down a number they are told. Even they find it awkward with long numbers.

b.v: About 30 minutes. The most useful lesson here.
Take the verb, drop -en, add the ending. machen (to do) becomes:
wir and sie/Sie always match the dictionary form. That is half the table done for free.
3) Two irregular ones you cannot avoid

v: haben: ich habe, du hast, er hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie haben
sein: ich bin, du bist, er ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie sind

b.v: Put the verb first. No extra word needed — German has no 'do you'.

v: Du sprichst Deutsch. → Sprichst du Deutsch?
Sie wohnen hier. → Wohnen Sie hier?
nicht after the verb: Ich arbeite nicht = I do not work
kein before a noun: Ich habe kein Geld = I have no money
Conjugate lernen and kaufen in full

b.v: halb vier means 'halfway to four', so 3:30. This trips up every English speaker at least once.
